noise:
None of the 48 random factors would have made it into the team, which needs help in at least 3 of the 4 years and an average gain of at least 0.01.

For pairs, the first rule ("beats the better one alone") let in 19 of 64 promising random pairs, about 30%. With the final rule (pair gain of at least 0.01, and at least 0.01 more than the two gains added up) it was 0 of 64 random pairs and only 1 of 64 promising ones.

Giving promising factors a second chance at the end let 1 of 18 random factors in, which is why that step is off. So anything that joins the team in B or C has done something random numbers almost never manage.
cards:
Each card has everything Dr Liu asked for: the formula, the gain in each year, LR vs RF, whether it was kept and why, how similar it is to the closest existing factor, the automatic "why" line, and Claude's own lesson from the next round.

Run C didn't select any factor, so the two examples here are a promising one and a rejected one.
prompt:
Claude clearly used the feedback. Its lessons are specific and mention particular years and models. For example, it worked out that smoothing volume over a few days "removed the one-day attention spike that carried the signal".

From round 2 onwards Claude also kept pointing out that nearly every factor helped in 2023 and 2025 and hurt in 2024. Step 9 shows that this is true for every kind of factor, not just Claude's.

Each round it gave 2 improve, 2 new and 2 partner factors, and labelled each one with a role (market condition, Apple-relative move, Apple's own pattern or peer lead).
run_c:
No factor made it into the team in this run. 14 ended up on the promising list, 33 were rejected, and 1 formula couldn't be used.

Claude gradually focused on trading-volume factors, such as Apple's volume surge compared with QQQ, NVIDIA or Microsoft. These gave the biggest gains on their own (up to +0.015), but only in 2 of the 4 years, nearly always 2023 and 2025.

There were 34 pair trials. The best pairs reached about +0.02, but none of them did more than +0.004 better than their two gains added up, so they stayed below the bar.

The whole run used about 97,000 input tokens and 13,000 output tokens, which is well under US$1.
run_b:
With the new rules, last week's 48 factors give a team of 4 instead of a single factor.

- **nvda_range_vs_aapl_range** is last week's factor. It joined in round 4.
- **msft_nvda_close_position_diff** was rejected last week because it only helped in 2 of 4 years on its own. On top of the team it helped in all 4 years (+0.014). This is the kind of factor Dr Liu said we were losing.
- **A pair** of an Apple-relative factor (NVIDIA vs Apple volatility) and a market factor (NVIDIA's range vs QQQ's range). Each was weak on the team (−0.001 and +0.004), but together they gave +0.013 in all 4 years, which is 0.010 more than the two added up. It's very close to Dr Liu's own example of a market-condition factor and an Apple-relative factor helping each other.
year_effect:
In 2023 about 80 to 90% of all factors improved the score, but in 2024 only 2 to 12% did. That happens with Claude's factors from both weeks and with the template formulas that had no LLM behind them at all.

So the rule "helped in 3 of 4 years" is partly measuring the years rather than the factors. In practice a factor has to win in 2022 or 2024, where almost nothing does.

I think the reason is how small each check is. One quarter is about 63 trading days, so luck is about as large as the effects we're looking for.
checks8:
With 8 checks, the bar (set with random numbers first) is at least 7 of 8 checks and an average gain of at least 0.0075. Only 2% of random factors and none of the template formulas pass it.

Only one family of Claude's factors is that consistent: a peer's daily price range compared with Apple's. The QQQ and Microsoft versions helped in 7 of 8 checks, and last week's NVIDIA version in 6 of 8.

This week's volume factors have the biggest average gains (up to +0.022), but they only help in 4 or 5 of the 8 checks. They're strong in some periods and do nothing in others.

Most of Claude's factors help in 4 or 5 of 8 checks, which is about what random numbers do. With this amount of data it's genuinely hard to find a factor that helps every time.
pile:
Out of 81 different factors (after removing near-copies of my 22), forward selection picks **qqq_range_vs_aapl_range**, which is QQQ's daily range minus Apple's. It helped in 7 of 8 checks. Nothing else passed the bar on top of it.

The pair trials are interesting though. A market volume factor (NVIDIA or QQQ volume surge) together with an Apple-relative volume factor gives +0.017 to +0.020, which is 0.005 to 0.009 more than the two added up, so they really do work better together. But they only helped in 6 of 8 checks, one short of the bar, so they weren't added. They would be good starting points for partner requests in the next run.
compare:
B (last week's factors with the team rules) did best. Compared with my 22 factors, Logistic Regression's test AUC went up by 0.040 (better in 3 of 4 years) and its balanced accuracy by 0.077, and Random Forest's balanced accuracy went up by 0.034. Last week's single factor (A) gave +0.031, +0.065 and +0.010.

B also earned the most in the backtest. On average per Q4, Logistic Regression made +3.2% (my 22 factors made −1.2%, A made +2.1%) and Random Forest made +6.3% (22 factors +4.0%, A +4.9%, buy-and-hold +4.9%).

P, the factor picked from the whole pile, was the most consistent in the checks, but its test gains are smaller. Logistic Regression's balanced accuracy went up by 0.033, while Random Forest got slightly worse (−0.022).

C didn't select anything, so it's the same as my 22 factors.

I'd be careful with these numbers. Each test quarter is only 63 days, and B's Random Forest AUC actually went down a little (−0.003), even though its balanced accuracy went up.
summary:
**What I built.** Following Dr Liu's feedback on 20 October, every factor now gets a report card, Claude writes a lesson about each one, new factors are tested on top of the selected team and in pairs, Claude is asked for partner factors, and everything is compared with last week. All the bars were set using random numbers before any real run.

**What worked.** Testing factors together keeps factors that last week's rule threw away. On last week's factors it built a team of 4, including a market factor and an Apple-relative factor that work as a pair, and that team beat last week's single factor on the final Q4 test (balanced accuracy for both models, and the backtest). Claude also clearly learns from the report cards. Its lessons are specific, and it found the year problem on its own.

**What I learned about the data.** Each year's check reacts to almost any factor in the same way: in 2023 nearly everything helps and in 2024 nearly everything hurts. Each check is only 63 days, so luck plays a big part, and that's why so few factors pass and why this week's Claude run didn't find a team member. With 8 checks instead of 4, the consistent factors are the "peer's range vs Apple's range" family, while Claude's volume factors are strong but unreliable. The random-number checks also caught four traps before they could fool me: lucky pairs, the forest changing at 25 factors, second chances, and grading on a curve.

**Next steps.**
- Use the 8 checks inside the loop, so Claude's report cards show the more reliable picture
- Repeat each method a few times to see how stable the chosen factors are
- Ask Claude for partners for the near-miss volume pairs (market volume with Apple-relative volume)
- Share the factor pile and the setting with the team, so others can try different feature selection methods on the same factors
